title: Spielberg has made some wonderful films, but Jaws is still his crowning achievement

commenti.body:
Eh jaws is good for sure but Jurassic Park imo is him at the peak of his powers. 

I don’t really value restraining sentimentality as priority in filmmaking the same way I don’t value restraining pessimism as one either. 

Art is about self expression. If it’s true to you, it’s good.

*Jaws* is absolutely a classic, and Shaw leads a strong cast. *Jaws* had the advantage of not being an art film, and not being a Spielberg-branded film, which is part of your point. 

It could be argued that there is some sentimentality in *Schindler's List* (the focus on the red jacket) or the entire premise of *Saving Private Ryan*. Even so, I don't see how we can place *Jaws* as being his "magnum opus" against pictures like these. 

*E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial* is actually *about* innocence and sentimentality, and it would be hard to love *Jaws* more than *E.T.* 

*A.I.: Artificial Intelligence* uses sentimentality as a blunt weapon, repeatedly smashing the audience square in the face with it. This is also a vastly more ambitious movie and, to me at least, is more meaningful than *Jaws*. 

For what it's worth, *Munich* is stone cold movie, and I can't think of anything sentimental about it at all.
Jurassic Park is absolutely his strongest in regards to special, action and suspense.

Rewatching *Raiders of the Lost Ark* after seeing *Dial of Destiny* recently, one huge difference that stood out is that there was a constant creativity in Raiders on a scene-by-scene basis that was missing in *Destiny*. Every scene in the 1981 film would have a creative gag, or an iconic shot, or a memorable line that would elevate a scene. And when you have a film full of those types of scenes you are three-quarters of the way to having a great film (they of course have to be structured in the right way to give a unified artistic whole.)

And the reason for that is the creativity of youth, when all a young director's cylinders are firing and their head is full of ideas and inspiration. It's the same reason most bands put out their best albums in their twenties and most scientists make their key discoveries early in their career.

Anyway, to get to the film at hand, *Jaws* has that scene-by-scene creativity even more so than Raiders. Every scene is perfect and full of that lateral-thinking creativity that delights an audience. Examples off the top of my head: the nails down the blackboard, Brody's son mirroring his hands, the kids in the water with the fake fin, the Vertigo shot on the beach, the number plate in the shark, "You're gonna need a bigger boat",  the U.S.S. Indianapolis, the old guys on the wharf, that one-shot on the ferry, the yellow barrels, the unseen shark with John William's iconic score, "Mary Ellen Moffit, she broke my heart", that jump scare on Ben Gardener's boat, the can-crushing scene, the ripped yellow kid's raft, the traumatized mother screaming at Brody, the vandalized billboard, "Smile, you Son of a Bitch" and more. It's just great scene after great scene.
Jurassic Park and Schindlers List in the same year. Dude was definitely at his peak.
[removed]

The things you cite - Shaw’s performance and the Indianapolis monologue were only indirectly influenced by Spielberg. (I believe his friend screenwriter and director John Milius wrote the Indianapolis monologue last minute.) That said, Jaws, Raiders and Jurassic Park for me are peak Spielberg-as-entertainer. The man can direct an action scene or a dialogue scene in a way that has momentum and propels the story forward. When the material he has to work with, in terms of actors and script, is great, the films are great.

Final note: John Williams also does plenty to create the magic we associate with Spielberg. Can you imagine Jaws with a different score?
Dial of Destiny wasn't directed by Spielberg, incidentally.

Jaws work, in part, because they kept having problems with the shark, so they had to keep making adjustments.  If they made that movie now, they would just CGI everything and it would be a very different movie.

I remember Stephen King saying something about how weird it is that people still tell him their favorite book is *The Stand.* They don't seem to realize how insulting it is to tell him that he peaked several decades ago.
*The Meg*?

Hmm...

There's a quote of Sir David Lean's that kinda sums up Jaws for me: "It made me jump quite a few times, but lets admit it, its not the greatest literature."

I prefer a loftier film, even if less impeccably-executed, to something more "perfect" but also more quixotic.

Pretentious, perhaps, but that's where I'm at, personally.
Great points, especially on Williams.

I almost can’t believe it was made by Spielberg until the bizarrely upbeat adventure score comes on during the shark hunt. It’s as though the sense of wonder he’s known for were completely replaced by cold dread, and it was fantastic for it, and all the adventure elements stood on their own without adornment: the harness they sit in to grip the pole, the barrel snagging, pure seafaring fun.

Shaw himself wrote the final version, taking bits of the 10 previous versions in the script. Just saw THE SHARK IS BROKEN, co-written by his son Ian(who looks and sounds uncannily like him), a pretty great hysterical on the backstage brawling between Shaw and Dreyfuss. 

 https://thedailyjaws.com/blog/2021/12/19/jaws-screenwriter-explains-story-behind-the-indianapolis-speech#:~:text=Actor%20Robert%20Shaw%20(Quint)%20is,screenplay)%20that%20conceived%20the%20idea.

Obligatory 'this is just my opinion'. 

I think Jurassic Park is entertaining as hell and the special effects are extraordinary, but it does not touch Jaws as a film imo.

The three main characters in Jaws are stronger than any characters in JP, so distinct and the way they play off each other is just wonderful. And the writing in Jaws is just so sharp. The Indianapolis scene is famous, but there are other great scenes like Quints intro, or the small exchange over dinner with Brody and his son.

I think the best way I could put it is you could take the shark out of jaws and id still be interested in watching whatever was left. Take the dinosaurs out of JP and you're not left with much else. I know that's an inherently silly way to describe it but that's the best I got.
Jaws is probably his best in terms of pure storytelling, but I do think Jurassic Park is the full maturation of his sensibilities. Both masterpieces.
I share this opinion as well

Jaws is probably my favorite of his. But I think Schindler's List will always be his most important. 

I don't agree with the criticisms I've read of it, and it's just pure aging to watch. But a film I think everyone should watch once. 

As far as the word 'masterpiece' goes, I'd also stick that label on Close Encounters and Raiders. Munich is ver close too.

Flawed but great, I'd put saving private Ryan, Jurassic park, catch me if you can, and minority report.

I don't remember ET we'll enough to rank it.

Dude has made a lot of great films.

AI is one of the Spielberg movies ive never seen oddly enough.. for some reason I wasn't really into minority report or Munich, and that movie came out around the same time and ive always lumped it in with those as a reason I never gave it a shot.

JAWS is one of my all-time favorite films, so I don't disagree with your ranking here. However, I'd like to point out that Spielberg has somewhat become a victim of the cynicism of his era. Some couldn't see the genuine sensibilities in some of his films, dismissing them as mere sentimental gimmicks or cheap tricks. This sentiment persisted among his critics for a long time. It's only in the last 20 years that he has received a kind of rehabilitation from serious critics. They also acknowledge that much of Spielberg's affection is rooted in the old storytelling of classical Hollywood, much like that of his peer, Peter Bogdanovitch.

Of all his film Jaws must be the most boring one he made lol 

I mean the dude made E.T, Indiana Jones, Catch me if you can, Schindlers list, Jurassic parc… etc etc, all those movies are literally 1000x better than Jaws.

Jaws is an amazing product of its time but doesn’t hold as much today.

I love Jaws but I think the best film Spielberg directed was Schindler's List. Schindler's List is nearly perfect in my estimation the only flaw I can find in it is honesty ultimately it's about life and the Holocaust was about death. Seeing as how most people probably won't watch Shoah I think that makes films like Schindler's List and The Pianist all the more significant. Though to be fair I'm a history nerd not filmmaker/cinephile.

‘Not the greatest literature’ is a strange criticism of a film that is essentially a retelling of Moby Dick. 

To that Spielberg adds a touch of cynicism about politics with the mayor opening the beach again despite Dreyfuss’ character proving the shark that was caught could not have killed the previous victims. 

I do like Jaws, but I think Minority Report is his perfect film, but I am a sucker for science fiction.

>To that Spielberg adds a touch of cynicism about politics with the mayor opening the beach again despite Dreyfuss’ character proving the shark that was caught could not have killed the previous victims.

That's true.

But still, I think Lean's point is well-taken.

I like Jaws. In Godard's history of cinema he argued Jaws spelt doom for cinema. Studios would favor more formulaic films and international cinema would become Americanized. I would put Raiders above it, but my favorite would be AI. Arguably Kubrick's influence prevented it from becoming mawkish.
I mean Godard is not wrong, Jaws was essentially the birth of the modern blockbuster. Amazing how prescient Godard was.

I think it kind of aged badly. The male protagonists feel so cliche to me. It's hard to overlook for me at this point. I acknowledge that it's great film making. But I find it hard to take it seriously tbh. Also it's hard to find it scary nowadays, which again is bad aging imho. And last but not least there's the whole thing about kicking off that myth of sharks being mean menaces and predators of humans. Which is really far off from the truth.

Jaws will forever be my favorite film.  The feeling of it. The behind the scenes problems and a young film geek just trying to make it all work.  Quint’s story about the Indianapolis and the way he told it commanded attention and attendance.  But that’s not all, that story brought fear into the viewer about what sharks can do and what we as prey just must accept.  

I like they got rid of the love triangle from the book.  

This is also why whenever my family goes anywhere for ice cream, I always ask for Coffee flavored.

Jaws started a series of monster thrillers.

But imo the best of Spielberg are Schindler's List, ET, Jurassic Park and Indiana Jones trilogy. The latter three are like the sequel of his own thriller/adventure series after Jaws, and paved the way for other series and franchises like Aliens and Avatars.

And Schindler's List is beyond everything else, it's an epic, a saga, more like the movie version of Les Miserables.
Oh, yeah, my brain turned off.

Munich is Spielberg's most overlooked film.  It's one of his five best films.

There's kind of an irony to it.  No one making Jaws at the time had any idea that it would become the phenomenon it became.  And, in a way, it kind of puts Spielberg in this odd place of both the unexpected creator of and, later, the most ardent evangelist of the modern blockbuster.

I've read that the more sentimental aspects of AI were very much part of Kubrick's original vision.  It was a departure for him.  And Spielberg actually reined much of that in to accentuate the deeper existential meanings.

Kubrick would have made the film with a robot if he could. Spielberg drew on Kubrick's material, but also Pinocchio and Super-Toys Last All Summer Long. I'd be surprised if a hypothetical Kubrick film would be more sentimental than this. But the Pinocchio allegory shows David's humanity. The inventor sees human drive to "see what isn't there" as the flaw of our species. 

I'm reminded of Zizek's idea that fantasy and ideology are more freeing than the authentic self. David chose to live with his robotic mother figure even after the real one discarded him. Like real children with abusive parents, David would rather blame himself than accept that his parents don't love him. 

After losing my mother, the idea that the spirit doesn't live on became unbearable. People dismiss myths as mere fairy tales. Someone like the inventor would see David's quixotic nature as foolish. But David is a good person with beliefs that sustain and guide him.
